title: diatheke
summary: These passages are connected by covenant, but they do not all make the same kind of statement. Genesis 9 recounts God’s promise to Noah; Deuteronomy 6 gives Israel instruction for covenant life; Jeremiah 31 promises a renewed covenant; Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah and relates that promise to Jesus’ ministry. The reader can follow how a prophetic promise is received in Hebrews while keeping the narrative and instruction passages distinct from that later argument.
historical_context: The references move from Genesis and Deuteronomy to Jeremiah and then to Hebrews’ interpretation of Jeremiah. The source list supports this textual sequence but does not include a lexicon or other research for detailed claims about the Greek term’s semantic range or its translation history.
canonical_context: Hebrews 8 directly quotes Jeremiah 31 and uses the promise of a new covenant in its argument. Genesis 9 and Deuteronomy 6 provide earlier covenant narratives and instruction, while Jeremiah supplies the promise Hebrews interprets. Those relationships are canonical and textual; they should not be mistaken for proof that every reference uses the same original-language word.
literary_context: The set includes a narrative promise, covenant instruction, prophetic speech, and a later letter’s scriptural argument. Hebrews’ quotation of Jeremiah is the clearest literary link in the list. Reading that quotation in context helps readers see how Hebrews develops the earlier promise rather than treating all four passages as interchangeable definitions.
covenantal_significance: The references connect promise, instruction, and renewal. Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant becomes a central text in Hebrews’ argument, while Genesis and Deuteronomy offer different covenant settings. This entry is best read through those textual relationships; a fuller account of the Greek term requires lexical support beyond the listed passages.
canonical_role: This entry gathers covenant passages, with Hebrews’ quotation of Jeremiah as its clearest New Testament link. It helps readers follow the argument across books while distinguishing a textual connection from a claim about identical word usage.
